title: Acoustical parameters for learning in classroom: A review
central_proposition: This review synthesizes empirical findings from 2002 to 2020 on classroom acoustics to propose specific acoustical parameter guidelines for optimizing student learning performance and well-being across different age groups.

concept_definitions.name: Speech Intelligibility
concept_definitions.definition: The percentage of correctly understood speech items with respect to the overall.

concept_definitions.name: Reverberation Time (Tmid)
concept_definitions.definition: The average reverberation time for the central octave bands (125 Hz to 4 kHz).

concept_definitions.name: A-weighted sound pressure level (LNeq)
concept_definitions.definition: The A-weighted sound pressure level of indoor noise acquired with students in silence or involved in classroom activities.

concept_definitions.name: Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR)
concept_definitions.definition: The ratio of speech signal level to background noise level.

concept_definitions.name: Speech Transmission Index (STI)
concept_definitions.definition: An objective measure of speech intelligibility, ranging from 0 (unintelligible) to 1 (perfect intelligibility).

concept_definitions.name: Informative Noise (IN)
concept_definitions.definition: Anthropic sound generated by talking people in the classroom or adjacent environments.

concept_definitions.name: Ambient Noise (AN)
concept_definitions.definition: Typical noises of the built environment (HVAC, traffic, classroom sounds like moving chairs, etc.).

concept_definitions.name: Listening Effort (LE)
concept_definitions.definition: The mental effort required to understand speech, especially in adverse acoustic conditions.

argument_structure: The paper systematically reviews empirical literature from 2002 to 2020 on classroom acoustics and student performance. It filters studies based on ecological validity and specific inclusion criteria, tabulates and analyzes data by age group (5-7, 8-11, 12+ years old) and performance outcome (better/worse). Finally, it synthesizes these findings into practical guidelines and thresholds for key acoustical parameters.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The review identifies that adverse acoustical conditions (high reverberation time, high noise levels, low SNR, low STI) increase listening effort, leading to prediction error in auditory processing (PP). This increased effort depletes cognitive resources, causing directed attention fatigue (DT) and impairing cognitive functions like short-term memory, sentence comprehension, and attention (MS, DT). Chronic exposure to poor acoustics also triggers stress responses (NM), leading to annoyance, discomfort, and reduced well-being (IC). Conversely, good acoustical conditions reduce listening effort, preserve cognitive resources, and support emotional well-being, thereby enhancing speech intelligibility, learning attainments, and overall student performance.

findings.antecedent: Classroom reverberation time (Tmid) for students under 12 years old
findings.mechanism: Lower reverberation time reduces speech masking and listening effort, improving speech intelligibility and cognitive processing, especially for younger children who are more susceptible to adverse acoustics.
findings.quote: Guidelines for better learning performance <12: Tmid 0.6
findings.empirical_support_cited: Studies [11,55,80,83] show higher accuracy in cognitive and intelligibility tasks with Tmid of 0.6 s for students aged 5-11.

findings.antecedent: Classroom reverberation time (Tmid) for students 12 years old and older
findings.mechanism: Lower reverberation time reduces speech masking and listening effort, improving speech intelligibility and cognitive processing. Older students have more developed cognitive abilities, allowing for slightly higher Tmid values compared to younger students while maintaining good performance.
findings.quote: Guidelines for better learning performance >12: Tmid 0.7
findings.empirical_support_cited: Studies [65,84] highlight good outcomes with Tmid of 0.7 s for students over 12 years.

findings.antecedent: Classroom background noise level (LNeq) for students under 12 years old
findings.mechanism: Lower noise levels reduce masking and cognitive load, decreasing listening effort and improving attention and comprehension. Younger children are more sensitive to noise.
findings.quote: Guidelines for better learning performance <12: LNeq <35
findings.empirical_support_cited: In accordance with Shield and Dockrell [16] and BB93 [25], where internal LNeq must be ≤35 dBA.

findings.antecedent: Classroom background noise level (LNeq) for students 12 years old and older
findings.mechanism: Lower noise levels reduce masking and cognitive load, decreasing listening effort and improving attention and comprehension. Older students can tolerate slightly higher noise levels due to more developed cognitive abilities.
findings.quote: Guidelines for better learning performance >12: LNeq <40
findings.empirical_support_cited: Picard & Bradley [23] proposed 40 dBA for this age range.

findings.antecedent: Classroom signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for students of all ages (5-40 years old)
findings.mechanism: Higher SNR ensures speech is sufficiently louder than background noise, reducing listening effort and improving speech intelligibility and comprehension across all age groups.
findings.quote: Guidelines for better learning performance <12: SNR ≥12; >12: SNR ≥12
findings.empirical_support_cited: Corroborates Picard & Bradley [23] finding that SNR >12 dBA is necessary for >80% speech intelligibility for students 6-12 y.o.

findings.antecedent: Classroom Speech Transmission Index (STI) for students under 12 years old
findings.mechanism: Higher STI indicates better speech intelligibility, which is crucial for younger children's developing linguistic and cognitive abilities, reducing their listening effort.
findings.quote: Guidelines for better learning performance <12: STI >0.65
findings.empirical_support_cited: Studies [3,12,18,91] show STI of 0.70 for better performance for subjects under 12 years.

findings.antecedent: Classroom Speech Transmission Index (STI) for students 12 years old and older
findings.mechanism: Higher STI indicates better speech intelligibility. Older students, with more developed cognitive abilities, can still achieve excellent intelligibility with slightly lower STI values compared to younger children.
findings.quote: Guidelines for better learning performance >12: STI >0.60
findings.empirical_support_cited: Studies [3,12,18,91] show STI of 0.67 for better performance for subjects 12 years or older.

findings.antecedent: Classroom reverberation time (Tmid) for students under 12 years old
findings.mechanism: Excessive reverberation time increases speech masking and listening effort, significantly impairing speech intelligibility and cognitive processing for younger children.
findings.quote: Thresholds for worse learning performance <12: Tmid ≥1.2
findings.empirical_support_cited: Derived from median values for worse performance in Table 4.

findings.antecedent: Classroom reverberation time (Tmid) for students 12 years old and older
findings.mechanism: Excessive reverberation time increases speech masking and listening effort, impairing speech intelligibility and cognitive processing. Older students can tolerate slightly higher Tmid before performance significantly degrades.
findings.quote: Thresholds for worse learning performance >12: Tmid ≥1.6
findings.empirical_support_cited: Derived from median values for worse performance in Table 4.

findings.antecedent: Classroom background noise level (LNeq) for students under 12 years old
findings.mechanism: High noise levels significantly increase masking and cognitive load, leading to increased listening effort, reduced attention, and impaired comprehension for younger children.
findings.quote: Thresholds for worse learning performance <12: LNeq ≥40
findings.empirical_support_cited: Derived from median values for worse performance in Table 4.

findings.antecedent: Classroom background noise level (LNeq) for students 12 years old and older
findings.mechanism: Very high noise levels significantly increase masking and cognitive load, leading to increased listening effort, reduced attention, and impaired comprehension, even for older students with more developed cognitive abilities.
findings.quote: Thresholds for worse learning performance >12: LNeq ≥60
findings.empirical_support_cited: Derived from median values for worse performance in Table 4.

findings.antecedent: Classroom signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for students under 12 years old
findings.mechanism: Low SNR means speech is not sufficiently louder than background noise, drastically increasing listening effort and severely impairing speech intelligibility and comprehension for younger children.
findings.quote: Thresholds for worse learning performance <12: SNR <5
findings.empirical_support_cited: Derived from median values for worse performance in Table 4.

findings.antecedent: Classroom signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for students 12 years old and older
findings.mechanism: Very low SNR means speech is significantly masked by background noise, drastically increasing listening effort and severely impairing speech intelligibility and comprehension, even for older students.
findings.quote: Thresholds for worse learning performance >12: SNR <-2
findings.empirical_support_cited: Derived from median values for worse performance in Table 4.

findings.antecedent: Classroom Speech Transmission Index (STI) for students under 12 years old
findings.mechanism: Low STI indicates poor speech intelligibility, which significantly hinders younger children's ability to understand spoken information and learn effectively.
findings.quote: Thresholds for worse learning performance <12: STI <0.65
findings.empirical_support_cited: Derived from median values for worse performance in Table 4.

findings.antecedent: Classroom Speech Transmission Index (STI) for students 12 years old and older
findings.mechanism: Low STI indicates poor speech intelligibility, which hinders older students' ability to understand spoken information and learn effectively, though they may tolerate slightly lower STI than younger children.
findings.quote: Thresholds for worse learning performance >12: STI <0.60
findings.empirical_support_cited: Derived from median values for worse performance in Table 4.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Classrooms designed with Tmid of 0.6 s, LNeq <35 dBA, SNR ≥12 dBA, and STI >0.65 will result in significantly better learning performance and well-being for students under 12 years old compared to classrooms exceeding these thresholds.

Classrooms designed with Tmid of 0.7 s, LNeq <40 dBA, SNR ≥12 dBA, and STI >0.60 will result in significantly better learning performance and well-being for students 12 years old and older compared to classrooms exceeding these thresholds.

Performance and well-being of non-mother tongue and hearing-impaired students will show differential sensitivity to acoustical parameters compared to normal-hearing, mother-tongue students, requiring more stringent guidelines.
bridge_warrants: The proposed guidelines update and expand upon previous benchmarks like Picard & Bradley (2001) by incorporating a wider range of performance measures (cognitive, subjective perception, beyond just intelligibility) and a more recent literature base.

The guidelines align with existing national and international acoustical standards for schools (e.g., ANSI/ASA 12.60-2010, Building Bulletin 93, AS/NZS 2107:2000, AIJES S001, SIS SS 25268:2007, UNI 11532-2) by providing specific parameter values derived from empirical evidence.

The findings support the concept that environmental features modulate cognitive resources (PP, DT) and physiological stress (NM), directly impacting task performance (T20) and subjective well-being (IC).
methodological_critiques: The search strategy's specific terms ('acoustic* AND measure*') may have limited the scope, potentially missing relevant papers using broader terms like 'acoustics' alone.
Unequal availability of data for certain acoustical parameters across different age groups led to varying robustness in the derived guidelines.
The review acknowledges the exclusion of vulnerable groups (non-mother tongue, hearing impaired, ASD students) from the final guideline derivation, highlighting a gap for future research.

The derived reference values are interrelated, but no theoretical calculations (e.g., based on diffuse field models) were performed to verify their coherence, which could be a limitation in design or verification phases.
model_structure: The paper does not propose a formal model but uses a PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome) strategy for literature search and a structured framework for data tabulation and analysis, categorizing studies by task (Intelligibility, Cognitive, Perception), performance measures, and age groups to derive empirical guidelines.
limitations: The review's scope was limited to studies published between 2002 and 2020.
Only studies with normal hearing subjects and typical lesson settings without amplification systems were included.
The guidelines are based on median values and personal assumptions by the authors, rather than complex analytical elaborations.
The study did not include non-mother tongue or hearing-impaired students, who may require different acoustic conditions.

paper_metadata.title: Reinforcement Learning: A Survey
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: This paper surveys the field of reinforcement learning from    a computer-science perspective. It is written to be accessible to    researchers familiar with machine learning.  Both the historical basis    of the field and a broad selection of current work are summarized.    Reinforcement learning is the problem faced by an agent that learns    behavior through trial-and-error interactions with a dynamic    environment.  The work described here has a resemblance to work in    psychology, but differs considerably in the details and in the use of    the word ``reinforcement.''  The paper discusses central issues of    reinforcement learning, including trading off exploration and    exploitation, establishing the foundations of the field via Markov    decision theory, learning from delayed reinforcement, constructing    empirical models to accelerate learning, making use of generalization    and hierarchy, and coping with hidden state.  It concludes with a    survey of some implemented systems and an assessment of the practical    utility of current methods for reinforcement learning.
